sections.h2: Where are Marion County property records kept?
sections.html:
The Marion County Clerk of Court and Comptroller keeps them. The clerk also serves as county recorder, so deeds, mortgages and liens all land in one general series called the Official Records.

The clerk's Official Records page describes the series as the place where instruments "required or authorized" by law are recorded and indexed once the statutory fees are paid. Its examples include deeds, mortgages, liens, contracts, affidavits, subdivision plats, declarations of condominium, bills of sale, judgments, military discharge certificates and declarations of domicile.

  • Department: Official Records, in the Clerk of Court Annex Building at 19 N Pine Avenue, Ocala, room 124.
  • Hours: Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 5:00 pm.
  • Direct phone: 352-671-5630.
  • Mail: Attn: Recording, P.O. Box 1030, Ocala, FL 34478-1030. For overnight mail, use 110 NW 1st Avenue, Ocala, FL 34475.

sections.h2: How do you search Marion County Official Records?
sections.html:
Use the clerk's online search, which is linked from the Official Records page and the clerk's site menu. The online options list also names a registration agreement for viewing records remotely and a form for registered users.

Finding the parcel first makes the search faster. The Marion County Property Appraiser offers a property search, a sales search and a map tool, and the Property Alert Service points owners to the appraiser's site to find a Parcel ID by owner name or site address. Search by party name or parcel, then read the instrument itself instead of relying on an index line.

For older material, the clerk's menu lists historic Official Records books for 1959 to 1964, a records center for research requests, and a page for plats and right-of-way documents. A public records request form is also under the clerk's contact menu.

sections.h2: What fees does the Marion County Clerk charge to record a document?
sections.html:
Fees follow section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes, and the clerk publishes an Official Records fee calculator on its site. The statute sets the base charge for an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches at $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page.

Clerk recording charges under Florida Statutes s. 28.24, as printed on the statute page
ChargeAmount
First page, instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches$5.00
Each additional page$4.00
Each name beyond four$1.00
Public Records Modernization Trust Fund, first page$1.00
Same fund, each additional page$0.50
Technology charge$4 per page, additional

The calculator is the safer way to price a particular filing, since a deed also carries the deed stamp tax and the clerk may apply other charges.

sections.h2: Does a Marion County deed owe documentary stamp tax?
sections.html:
Usually yes. Florida taxes a deed at 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, and consideration counts money, the discharge of an obligation and any mortgage or encumbrance on the property, assumed or not.

Florida's revenue department says every party to the document is liable regardless of which party agrees to pay. The clerk collects the tax when the document is recorded. Warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's and life estate deeds are on the list of taxable deeds, as are deeds in lieu of foreclosure and certificates of title. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable.

  • Spousal homestead deeds where the only consideration is a mortgage, and divorce deeds for the marital home, are exempt under section 201.02(7).
  • The department says there is no specific exemption for estate planning transfers.
  • A lady bird deed was treated as not taxable in one department advisement on the facts presented there.

Ask the title company or an attorney how these rules fit a specific Marion County transfer.

sections.h2: Can you record a Marion County deed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes, but only through a third-party vendor. The clerk's e-recording page says documents for eRecording must be submitted through one of the approved vendors, and the clerk cannot recommend or endorse any of them.

The page names CSC eRecording Solutions, eRecording Partners Network, Hopdox and Simplifile, each with its own contact. The clerk's pitch for the service is saving the cost of checks, mailing and runners, and keeping the original document in your hands. A title company normally records for you at closing, so owners rarely need to set up an account.

Paper documents go to the Official Records department by mail or in person at the addresses above, with the statutory fees.

sections.h2: How can a Marion County owner watch for property fraud?
sections.html:
Sign up for the clerk's Property Alert Service. It emails you when a document is recorded that matches a Parcel ID or party name you register, and the clerk says it does not prevent fraud, only alerts you to it.

The signup steps are: register a username and password, click the link in the confirmation email, then choose Parcel IDs or party names. For names, the clerk suggests entering several variations, written last name first, such as Smith John, Smith John A and Smith John Allen, with suffixes added at the end.

If an alert shows an unauthorized transaction, the service tells you to contact law enforcement and to take legal action if you consider it warranted. Sellers who are away from the house for long stretches, or who inherited a home, gain the most from the alerts.

sections.h2: Why do Marion County records matter before a sale?
sections.html:
The records show what a buyer or title company will find: the vesting deed, mortgages, liens, judgments and any recorded easements or plats. Pull them early so you can clear problems before closing.

Property tax also ties back to the records. The tax collector and the clerk both handle later stages of delinquent taxes, since the clerk lists tax deed sales and lands available for taxes among its departments. Florida's revenue department notes that the clerk is the officer who runs tax deed sales and collects deed stamp tax at recording. Check the tax collector's page for any certificate on the parcel.

faqs.q: Who records deeds in Marion County?
faqs.a: The Marion County Clerk of Court and Comptroller, who is the county recorder. Recorded instruments go into the Official Records.

faqs.q: Where is the Marion County Official Records office?
faqs.a: In the Clerk of Court Annex Building at 19 N Pine Avenue, Ocala, room 124. It is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 am to 5:00 pm, and the direct number is 352-671-5630.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a document in Marion County?
faqs.a: The statute sets $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, plus other charges such as the modernization fund and technology fees. Use the clerk's fee calculator for a specific document.

faqs.q: Can I e-record in Marion County?
faqs.a: Yes, through an approved third-party vendor listed on the clerk's e-recording page. The clerk does not endorse any vendor.

faqs.q: Is there a way to be alerted when someone records a document against my property?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk's Property Alert Service sends alerts for registered Parcel IDs and party names. It does not block fraud.
